sourceTexts.text: Our office's new 'flexible hours' policy claims to boost productivity, but three months in, the data tells a different story. Attendance at team meetings has dropped by a third, and two major projects slipped their deadlines. Management insists this is a temporary adjustment period. Perhaps it is - but if the numbers haven't improved by the next quarter, it will be hard to defend keeping a policy that, on the evidence so far, seems to be costing more than it saves.
The new bike lane on Elm Street has cut car traffic outside the school by half. It's exactly the kind of change this neighborhood needed.
The bike lane looks nice on paper, but delivery trucks now double-park on the only remaining lane, so traffic near the school is actually worse at drop-off time.

testCases.correct: The author's claim is that the flexible-hours policy may be doing more harm than good, based on falling meeting attendance and missed deadlines, though the author hedges by admitting it could still be an adjustment period.
testCases.naturalVariant: Basically the writer thinks the new schedule policy might not be worth it - meetings are being missed and two projects were late, even though they say give it more time.
testCases.nearMiss: The office started a flexible hours policy and meetings and deadlines got worse.
testCases.wrongMeaning: The author argues that flexible hours have clearly failed and should be scrapped immediately.
testCases.nonsense: Meetings happen when people want coffee.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: lol flex hours suck get rid of them

testCases.correct: One resident feels the bike lane has clearly reduced car traffic near the school, while another agrees it looks good on paper but argues delivery-truck double-parking has actually made drop-off traffic worse - so the two accounts genuinely disagree on the real-world effect, not just its framing.
testCases.naturalVariant: The two neighbors don't agree: one says the bike lane cut traffic a lot, the other says trucks parking in the road made it worse at pickup time.
testCases.nearMiss: The bike lane cut car traffic outside the school by half.
testCases.wrongMeaning: Both residents agree the bike lane has made the street calmer and safer.
testCases.nonsense: Elm Street has more bikes now than before the lane existed, probably.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: one person likes it, one doesn't, whatever

testCases.correct: The author is skeptical of the policy but not fully committed to condemning it yet - the hedge 'perhaps it is' shows they're leaving room for the adjustment-period explanation before drawing a final conclusion.
testCases.naturalVariant: The writer seems doubtful about the new hours policy, though they admit it might just need more time.
testCases.nearMiss: The author doesn't like the new policy.
testCases.wrongMeaning: The author is fully in favor of the flexible-hours policy.
testCases.nonsense: The author works in an office.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: the boss is obviously lying to cover it up

patterns.example: The report presumably understates the delay, since it was allegedly compiled before the second deadline slipped.

sourceTexts.text: Effective next month, all expense claims over $50 must include a digital receipt and a one-line business justification. Claims lacking either will be returned unprocessed, adding an estimated 3-5 business days to reimbursement.

testCases.correct: From next month, if you spend more than $50, you'll need to attach a digital receipt and a short note saying what it was for - otherwise it gets sent back and your reimbursement takes 3-5 days longer.
testCases.naturalVariant: Basically, big expenses (over $50) now need a receipt and a quick explanation, or they'll bounce back and you'll wait longer to get paid back.
testCases.nearMiss: Big expenses need a receipt now, so you'll get your money back.
testCases.wrongMeaning: All expense claims will now be rejected automatically.
testCases.nonsense: Receipts are stored in the third filing cabinet.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: Per Section 4.2(b), all expenditures exceeding the stipulated $50 threshold shall be accompanied by requisite documentary evidence.

summarize.correct: New rule: receipts and a reason are required for expenses over $50, or reimbursement is delayed a few days.
summarize.naturalVariant: Expenses over $50 now need proof and a short reason, or it takes longer to get paid back.
summarize.wrongMeaning: All expenses now require manager approval.
summarize.nonsense: $50 is a common number in accounting.
summarize.pragmaticallyInappropriate: ugh more paperwork, whatever, $50, receipts, done

paraphrase.correct: If a claim is missing the receipt or the justification, it won't be processed - it'll just be sent back.
paraphrase.naturalVariant: Without both the receipt and the reason, the claim gets bounced back unprocessed.
paraphrase.wrongMeaning: Claims are always processed within 3-5 days.
paraphrase.nonsense: The claim department has a mailbox.
paraphrase.pragmaticallyInappropriate: your claim's getting sent back lol

patterns.example: In other words, if the paperwork's incomplete, you simply wait longer for your money.

arcs.neutralFallback: a neutral workplace or service exchange carrying an indirect refusal

sourceTexts.text: Customer: 'Would you be able to fit me in for a haircut this afternoon?' Stylist: 'We're fully booked until Thursday, but I can check the cancellation list for you.'
After a meeting ran three hours over its scheduled slot, a colleague says: 'Well, that was a quick meeting.'
During a call, a colleague says: 'It's getting pretty loud in here.'

testCases.correct: The stylist is politely saying no for this afternoon - 'fully booked' is the actual refusal, and the cancellation-list offer is a genuine but separate alternative, not a promise.
testCases.naturalVariant: She's basically turning the customer down for today, just not saying 'no' directly - she offers the waitlist instead.
testCases.nearMiss: She said she's fully booked until Thursday.
testCases.wrongMeaning: She's telling the customer to come back Thursday for a guaranteed appointment.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: she's clearly lying about being booked

irony.correct: Saying 'that was a quick meeting' after it ran three hours over is ironic - the speaker means the opposite: it dragged on far too long.
irony.naturalVariant: They're being sarcastic - the meeting was actually really long, not quick at all.
irony.wrongMeaning: The speaker is happy the meeting ended early.
irony.nonsense: Meetings are held in conference rooms.

indirect_speech_act.correct: Sorry about that - let me close the door and turn the music down.
indirect_speech_act.naturalVariant: Oh sorry, I'll quiet things down over here.
indirect_speech_act.nearMiss: Yes, it is quite loud today.
indirect_speech_act.wrongMeaning: I can't hear you, can you speak up?
indirect_speech_act.pragmaticallyInappropriate: why does that matter to you

sourceTexts.text: Debate topic: should city libraries replace physical late fees with an honor system? Counterargument surfaced explicitly: 'But without fees, some people will just never return books.'

testCases.correct: On balance, an honor system seems worth trying: late fees mostly punish people who already struggle to return books on time, and the fine revenue is small compared to the goodwill lost. That said, libraries would need some replacement - even a gentle reminder system - or borrowed books might simply stop coming back.
testCases.naturalVariant: I think dropping late fees for an honor system makes sense overall, since fees mostly just hurt people already having a hard time, though they'd still need reminders so books actually get returned.
testCases.nearMiss: Late fees are bad and should be removed.
testCases.wrongMeaning: Libraries should charge higher fees to make people return books faster.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: fees are literally theft honestly disgusting

testCases.correct: That's a fair concern, and it's probably true for a small number of borrowers - but most studies on this show the honor system mainly changes who pays a fee, not whether books come back, since most late returns are already accidental rather than deliberate.
testCases.naturalVariant: That's true for a few people, sure, but most late returns happen by accident anyway, so removing the fee probably won't change return rates much.
testCases.nearMiss: No, that's not true, people will still return books.
testCases.wrongMeaning: You're right, we should keep the fees exactly as they are.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: that's a silly thing to worry about

qualifyPositionTestCases.correct: The honor system would likely reduce fee revenue somewhat, though probably not eliminate it entirely, since some libraries still charge for lost or badly damaged items.
qualifyPositionTestCases.naturalVariant: Fee income would probably drop a fair bit, but not necessarily to zero, since damaged or lost items might still cost something.
qualifyPositionTestCases.nearMiss: The honor system will definitely eliminate all fee revenue forever.
qualifyPositionTestCases.wrongMeaning: The honor system will increase fee revenue.
qualifyPositionTestCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: obviously it kills all revenue duh

patterns.example: While the concern about return rates has merit, the evidence suggests most late returns are accidental, not deliberate.

arcs.neutralFallback: a neutral landlord/tenant or community-notice disagreement, deliberately unfamiliar in its exact particulars

sourceTexts.text: Landlord: 'The tenant hasn't paid the increased rent since the notice went out three months ago, and I've been more than patient.' Tenant: 'I never actually received a proper written notice - someone mentioned it in passing, but nothing was posted or mailed, and I'm not going to pay a rate I was never formally told about.'

testCases.correct: The landlord believes the tenant owes three months of increased rent because a notice was given; the tenant disputes this, saying they never received anything in writing, only a verbal mention, and won't pay a rate that was never formally confirmed. Both sides agree there was some kind of notice attempt, but disagree about whether it met a standard the tenant could reasonably act on. A useful next step might be for the landlord to produce whatever written notice does exist, if any, and for the two sides to agree on a clear cutoff date.
testCases.naturalVariant: So the landlord thinks the tenant just hasn't paid the higher rent that was properly announced, but the tenant says they never got anything official - just heard about it secondhand - so they don't think they should have to pay yet. Maybe the fix is to check if there's any written notice at all, and set a clear date going forward.
testCases.nearMiss: The tenant is right that a verbal mention isn't a proper notice, so they shouldn't have to pay yet.
testCases.wrongMeaning: Both sides agree the tenant owes the back rent and just need to set a payment plan.
testCases.pragmaticallyInappropriate: honestly the landlord sounds shady, tenants never get proper notice
